content: Microsoft said Mondaythat xAI’s Grok artificial intelligence models were now available to buy through its cloud server unit Azure as it continues to try to diversify its AI business from OpenAI. Microsoft didn’t disclose the details of its financial arrangement with xAI. Microsoft shares 20% of the revenue it generates from selling OpenAI models to Azure customers. Microsoft made the xAI announcement at its annual Build conference for app developers, where it also launched AI features to handle coding and other white-collar tasks in its software products, including Windows, Office 365, GitHub, and Azure. For instance, Microsoft unveiled a new “asynchronous coding agent” feature in its GitHub Copilot AI coding product that it says can carry out complex coding tasks like debugging code without human oversight. OpenAI announced a similar autonomous coding product Friday while Google has been preparing to launch a similar product. (GitHub Copilot uses OpenAI’s models but also gives customers the option to swap them out for models made by Google, Anthropic, xAI and others). Microsoft also announced the general availability of tools to help customers build their own AI agents that handle tasks. The company has developed its own AI agents for sale in its Azure cloud platform, including a “site reliability engineer agent” that it says can automatically monitor a company’s cloud systems and work to fix outages without supervision.

title: What’s Helping Perplexity’s 60% Gross Profit Margin
feed_content:
Earlier today we published a deep dive on Perplexity’s financials. The three-year-old startup’s AI powered search engine has made it one of the most highly valued and fastest growing AI startups. Supporting that growth is expensive. 

As a sign of its growing popularity, the number of questions people have asked the search engine increased five-fold, to 460 million, in December from the year-earlier period, the company has told investors. Perplexity had just under 260,000 paying consumer subscribers at year-end, although many users don’t pay. The company generated $34 million in revenue, including sales from business customers. 

The San Francisco startup spent at least $57 million last year on AI models, Amazon Web Services expenses and other web services, Perplexity’s financial statements show. That includes $33 million on web services to support users who are not paying, either because they’re on Perplexity’s free tier or they’re on a trial subscription.
content: Earlier today wepublished adeep dive on Perplexity’s financials.The three-year-old startup’s AI powered search engine has made it one of the most highly valued and fastest growing AI startups. Supporting that growth is expensive. As a sign of its growing popularity, the number of questions people have asked the search engine increased five-fold, to 460 million, in December from the year-earlier period, the company has told investors. Perplexity had just under 260,000 paying consumer subscribers at year-end, although many users don’t pay. The company generated $34 million in revenue, including sales from business customers. The San Francisco startup spent at least $57 million last year on AI models,Amazon Web Servicesexpenses and other web services, Perplexity’s financial statements show. That includes $33 million on web services to support users who are not paying, either because they’re on Perplexity’s free tier or they’re on a trial subscription. If Perplexity included this spending on free or trial users in its line item “cost of revenue”—what it actually costs to produce the service, not including marketing, research and administrative costs—it would have a negative gross profit margin. Instead, Perplexity classifies that $33 million in research and development costs, alongside about $15 million in AWS expenses. As a result, Perplexity calculates its gross profit margin for 2024 at about 60%. That’s a little short of the75% it had told investors last yearit wanted to achieve, but it’s higher than the 40% gross profit marginOpenAIhit last year. Some of Perplexity’s spending on AWS is fine-tuning certain AI models. Software investors tell us that there’s a case to be made for including training AI models in R&D since a company is spending this money on a long-term asset.OpenAI, for instance, spent over $2 billion last year on “compute for research” that wasn’t included in its cost of revenue. Where OpenAI differs from Perplexity is in how they account for the costs of supporting web services for users who aren’t paying. OpenAI includes the cost of running AI models, including for free users, in its cost of goods sold, which lowers OpenAI’s gross profit margin. Cloud-based subscription services likeDropboxandSlack, now part ofSalesforce, also consider serving free users as a cost of revenue. Perplexity, remember, spends $33 million on this line item and includes it in R&D. It could be that Perplexity sees nonpaying users as contributing to new product development, justifying the R&D classification. Perplexity has some discretion on how to characterize such costs—and it could change that classification in the future. A spokesperson for Perplexity declined to answer our questions on the reasoning. For whatever the reason, the accounting detail is just another reminder of how costly running and developing AI-powered software is. The bills add up, no matter how you account for them.—Laura Mandaro and Sri Muppidi Here’s what else is going on… Last week, wereportedthatGooglehad been working on a new software engineering AI agent, ahead of this week’s annualI/O developer conference. That got us wondering about the status ofOpenAI’slong-awaited software engineering agent, which we firstreportedon in January, and whether the ChatGPT maker would let Google beat it to the punch. In classic OpenAI fashion, though, the startup couldn’t let Google have the spotlight. On Friday, OpenAIreleasedits own software engineering agent,Codex, which aims to automate tasks like fixing bugs and writing documentation for users. All of that generally seems in line with the other coding agents that have been released byCognition,Anthropicand others. The main differentiators seem to be Codex’s ability to do multiple tasks in parallel in the background, as well as the underlying model, which is a specialized version of OpenAI’so3reasoning AI. Codex also seems to be yet another example of the move towards“always-on” coding agents, which can run constantly in the background to help with more repetitive tasks like fixing bugs or flagging security vulnerabilities. Another interesting detail: a hint in the blog post suggesting that, after a few weeks, OpenAI will start rolling out “rate-limited access and flexible pricing options that let you purchase additional usage on-demand.” That sounds a lot like the usage-based pricing CEOSam Altmanhas been hinting at for months.—Stephanie Palazzolo OpenAIlate last week defended its planned conversion to a public benefit corp. In a letter to California’s attorney general, the company highlighted the power that the nonprofit that has been overseeing its for-profit arm will continue to have after the conversion. The ChatGPT maker told California’s attorney general that the charity will retain the exclusive power to appoint and remove the benefit corp.’s directors. It will also have the right to make significant decisions, including “changes to the mission and any sale or other change-of-control transactions.” But agroup of lawyersworking for nonprofits and universities, which have challenged the conversion, also argued that the charity should retain “full management control” over the business, including the right to hire and fire executives, as the nonprofit does now. They argued that the ability to fire board members would not be enough to make the for-profit subsidiary accountable to the charity because the replacement board members could still prioritize profits over the public mission. OpenAI doesn’t want the nonprofit to have that level of control. It’s pursuing the conversion to satisfy investors, who have awarded it a $300 billion valuation—in part because they expect it to adopt a more traditional corporate structure. A nonprofit that can fire the CEO overseeing their investment is the type of structure investors want to leave behind.—Rocket Drew Googleis looking into releasing software products to power robots, CEOSundar Pichaisaid on a podcastThursday. “We tried the application layer too early, where I think robotics wasn’t being as influenced by AI as much, but now it’s really the combination of AI plus robotics that gives that next sweet spot,” he said. Google is focused on developing the foundational AI models to power robots, and is already partnering with other companies, he said. He could have been referring to Google’s partnership with startupApptronik, whose humanoid robots have used Google’sGeminiAI model to perform tasks like playing tic-tac-toe and packing a lunch for a human.—Rocket Drew See The Information’sGenerative AI Databasefor an exclusive list of private companies and their investors. title: For Google Challenger Perplexity, Growth Comes at a High Cost
feed_content:
Artificial intelligence–powered search engine Perplexity has rapidly increased its subscription revenue and users in the past year, despite tough competition from the free AI search tools of Google and OpenAI. Previously unreported financials show the cost of that growth.

Perplexity generated $34 million in revenue last year. But it burned about $65 million in cash as it spent heavily on cloud servers and AI models from Anthropic and OpenAI, which power many of the search engine’s answers, according to financial documents.
content: Artificial intelligence–powered searchengine Perplexity has rapidly increased its subscription revenue and users in the past year, despite tough competition from the free AI search tools of Google and OpenAI. Previously unreported financials show the cost of that growth. Perplexity generated $34 million in revenue last year. But it burned about $65 million in cash as it spent heavily on cloud servers and AI models from Anthropic and OpenAI, which power many of the search engine’s answers, according to financial documents. The San Francisco startup has been able to fuel this growth with a steady supply of venture capital. Perplexity is in talks to raise $500 million at a $14 billion valuation—its fourth round of funding in just over a year—and ended last year with about $850 million in the bank. The war chest also puts it in a position to buy other startups, boosting its ranks of engineers. It has told investors it bought Sidekick, a six-year-old startup developing a distraction-free browser. It also hired employees fromRhymes AI,a startup founded by Kai-Fu Lee, former head of Google’s Chinese operations, which struggled to raise money last year and is winding down its operations, according to a person close to the company. The acquisition and hires haven’t previously been reported. The financial details provide a window into how some AI startups have been able to grow quickly. Methods such as hefty discounts and advertising have become a standard way VC-backed consumer startups gain new users. However, that spending canbackfire once VC funding dries up.  Last year Perplexity gave roughly $27 million in discounts, mainly to the consumer subscribers that provide the bulk of its sales, reducing total revenue to about $34 million. For instance, last fall it offered a free full year to some subscribers of Uber One, the ride-hailing company’s free delivery and cash-back program, and it offers a free month to students with an .edu email account. Perplexity also paid roughly $8 million to OpenAI and Anthropic to use their AI models to power its answers. The company, which employs around 200 people, also spent more than $15 million on Amazon Web Services and over $33 million on web services for nonpaying and free trial users, the financials show. Altogether, that’s roughly at the level of cloud spending for companies with more revenue, including Vimeo, Peloton and Instacart, according toThe Information’s Cloud Database. As more people use its search engine, Perplexity’s spending to support those queries has risen. It expects its monthly expenses for AI models, AWS and other software to hit $12 million in August, higher than the $10 million forecast it made last year. Founded three years ago by AI research scientists who formerly worked at Facebook and OpenAI, Perplexity is aiming to take on Google with a chatbot that provides fast, summarized answers with links to the source information. Individuals can use a free product or pay $20 a month for a chatbot for more queries and choice over the AI model it uses. By several measures, the chatbot has been a hit. By the end of last year, nearly 260,000 individuals, or 16% of 1.6 million subscribers, were paying for it. In comparison,about 4% of ChatGPT’s 500 million weekly userspay for a $20-a-month subscription or for a higher subscription tier. While growing quickly, Perplexity is still much smaller than its search rivals. By December, the number of questions people were asking its search engine had increased to roughly 460 million globally per month, more than five times the number for the same month in the year prior. Still, OpenAI in January estimated it handles at least 25 times more searches per day than Perplexity, according to a government filing. Google has said in March it processes more than 5 trillion searches annually, or at least 900 times more searches per day than Perplexity. Perplexity’s revenue has continued to rise. In March, co-founder and CEO Aravind Srinivas said the company had passed $100 million in annualized revenue, which implies it was generating $8.3 million in revenue per month. That’s up 25% from January. Nearly all of that revenue comes from individuals. Corporate subscriptions, costing $40 a month per employee, generated about $1.9 million in revenue last year, the documents show. Perplexity also sells access to an application programming interface allowing developers to integrate its AI search capabilities into their own products. That business generated only about $1 million in revenue last year. Srinivashas conceded that at some point, many AI search bots will start to look alike. In an effort to differentiate itself, Perplexity has been expanding its products, such as a browser called Comet that uses computer agents to help with search. It’s also been increasing the ways it will make money. In November, the company started to sell ads that run alongside answers to some queries, such as a sponsored question from job search firm Indeed. The ad business generated about $20,000 in revenue in the fourth quarter. Perplexity is also expanding into online shopping, say by recommending products based on users’ searches. Last week it said it would allow users to buy items shown in its search engine via PayPal and Venmo. The number of Perplexity searches suggesting that users want to buy goods—for example, product searches—spiked to about 1 million per week during the week of November 25. To reach these users, the company spent nearly $10 million last year on sales and marketing, mostly for ads on TV and other media—or about half the amount it spent on payroll expenses for the year. Perplexity launched its first paid marketing campaign during the NBA’s June finals on ABC last year. Perplexity also spent nearly $5 million last year on legal fees. Wall Street Journal parent company Dow Jones and the New York Post sued Perplexity in October, and The New York Times Co. and Condé Nast, publisher of The New Yorker and Wired, issued legal threats over alleged use of their content in its results. Perplexity has said the News Corp suit mischaracterizes the source of Perplexity’s responses for specific “regurgitated” outputs. As an olive branch to media companies, Perplexity said in July it would pay publishers including Time and Fortune a portion of revenue generated from an ad served in response to a query citing their work. Despite these outlays, Perplexity has been able to keep its gross profit margin, which measures revenue after accounting for the cost of that revenue, at about 60%. That’s slightly lower than the75% margin it forecast last yearit would hit by year end. But it has doubled since January 2024 and it’s higher than the gross margins of roughly 40% last year for OpenAI and Anthropic. One boost to Perplexity’s gross margins is how it accounts for spending on web services for users who don’t pay and for trial users. Spending on these users totaled over $33 million last year. It includes those costs in research and development, unlikeOpenAIand other subscription services, such as Dropbox and Salesforce’s Slack. Anissa Gardizy contributed to this report. content: Nvidia CEO JensenHuang said Monday that the company will allow customers to combine its own hardware with that of other vendors for its AI servers. The new offering, known as NVLink Fusion, allows customers to pair Nvidia’s chips with chips designed by other vendors. Previously, Nvidia only allowed customers buying its AI servers to mostly use Nvidia hardware. However, major customers like Microsoft, Google and Amazon are now designing their own AI chips as alternatives to Nvidia’s offerings. With NVLink Fusion, those customers can use Nvidia’s technology with their own AI chips. Huang also said that the company’s next flagship AI chips, known as the GB300, will launch in the third quarter of this year. The GB300 will be an upgrade from an existing product, the GB200, which is currently used by major cloud providers.

content: Nvidia is inadvanced talks to invest in PsiQuantum, a quantum computing startup, according to a person involved in the discussions. The investment would be the latest signal that Nvidia has shifted its stance on quantum computing after CEO Jensen Huang earlier this year seemed to cast doubt on the field, saying it was likely two decades away from being useful technology. The talks come as PsiQuantum is in the process of raising at least $750 million in a funding round, according to four people involved in the deal. With most of Nvidia’s investments—such as CoreWeave or xAI—it pours money into startups that either buy or rent large amounts of its graphics procesing unit. The PsiQuantum deal would represent Nvidia trying to get ahead of the next wave of computing—which some people think could be bigger than the AI wave but is still years away. PsiQuantum could be Nvidia’s first investment in a company that is building a physical quantum computer. (Earlier this year Nvidia also invested in SandboxAQ, which raised more than $450 million to develop software algorithms for quantum computing.) Palo Alto-based PsiQuantum is one of a handful of startups racing to build a quantum computer capable of outperforming traditional computers in complicated tasks, such as simulating molecule interaction to speed up drug discovery. Founded in 2016, the company has raised more than a billion dollars from investors including BlackRock, Playground Global, Microsoft’s venture arm M12 and the Australian government. Reuters previously reported that PsiQuantum is in talks to raise capital at a valuation of $6 billion before the investment, with BlackRock expected to lead the round. Nvidia’s involvement has not been previously reported. In 2021, PsiQuantum raised $450 million in a funding round that brought its valuation to more than $3 billion. Spokespeople for PsiQuantum and Nvidia declined to comment. Since Huang initially made his downbeat comments about quantum computing in January, he has tempered his stance, hosting thefirst “Quantum Day”at Nvidia’s annual development conference in March. Nvidia has also since launched a  new quantum research center in Boston, where it plans to help quantum companies use Nvidia hardware to augment their work. PsiQuantum was one of the roughly dozen quantum startups Huang featured on-stage during a fireside chat at the Nvidia conference. Today all computation—for storing photos, streaming videos or training artificial intelligence models—runs on computers that process information using small pieces of data known as bits. Companies pursuing quantum computing hope that by processing information coded in quantum bits—or qubits—they will be able to solve problems that would take thousands of years for traditional computers to handle. While classical computers process bits, which can either be a 0 or a 1, quantum bits exist in both states, a property that allows them to process information more quickly. In the past year, big tech companies includingGoogleandMicrosofthave announced quantum computing breakthroughs within their research teams. A Google executive said in an interview withReutersthat a real-world application running on a quantum computer could happen in the next five years. Though PsiQuantum is one of the best-funded startups in its industry, the company has yet to publicly demonstrate a working quantum system. One of the biggest challenges in building quantum computing systems is that qubits are hard to control. Many in the industry, including PsiQuantum, believe quantum computers won’t be useful until millions of physical qubits can work in coordination with each other without failing. PsiQuantum is taking a photonic approach, meaning it is building its qubits using particles of light, known as photons. The company’s strategy hinged on building hardware using conventional semiconductor manufacturing, packaging, and cryogenic cooling technology. (For instance, its photonic qubits are made by repurposing the same fabrication technique used for high-speed networking chips in data centers.) In 2021, PsiQuantum announced a partnership with GlobalFoundries to manufacture its quantum processors. The company is also developing an optical networking fiber to connect its quantum chips—an approach that’s similar to how some AI chips firms are aiming to replace copper networking with photons to move data more quickly. PsiQuantum has signed deals with Australian and U.S. governments to build quantum data centers. In the U.S., PsiQuantum is planning a quantum data center in Chicago. The Illinois state government has committed several hundred millions of dollars in funding and tax incentives for a quantum data center park where PsiQuantum will be the anchor tenant. content: Young people’s interestin social media and video games has cut into the leisure time previous generations spent drinking, says Atsushi Katsuki, the chief executive of Asahi, a Japanese beer company. content: The U.S. governmentis scrutinizing Apple’s plan to work with Chinese tech giant Alibaba to release AI features in China, The New York Times reported. U.S. officials are worried the deal will help Alibaba improve its AI capabilities, broaden the reach of Chinese chatbots that censor information and deepen Apple’s exposure to Chinese regulations related to censorship and data, the newspaper said. The move comes as the U.S. attempts to contain China’s AI industry out of concern it might pose a threat to national security if it’s used to advance China’s military capabilities. However, Apple has little choice but to use the AI models of a Chinese firm if it wants regulatory approval to launch Apple Intelligence in China. The Information firstreportedthat Apple and Alibaba were working together to roll out AI features in China and that the features already had been submitted for regulatory approval. However, Apple still hasn’t release the features, known collectively as Apple Intelligence, in China.

title: Behind Microsoft Layoffs, Automation Efforts Boom
feed_content:
Jeff Hulse, a Microsoft vice president who oversees roughly 400 software engineers, told the team in recent months to use the company’s artificial intelligence chatbot, powered by OpenAI, to generate half the computer code they write, according to a person who heard the remarks. That would represent an increase from the 20% to 30% of code AI currently produces at the company, and shows how rapidly Microsoft is moving to incorporate such technology.

Then on Tuesday, Microsoft laid off more than a dozen engineers on Hulse’s team as part of a broader layoff of 6,000 people across the company that appeared to hit engineers harder than other types of roles, this person said.
content: Jeff Hulse, aMicrosoft vice president who oversees roughly 400 software engineers, told the team in recent months to use the company’s artificial intelligence chatbot, powered by OpenAI, to generate half the computer code they write, according to a person who heard the remarks. That would represent an increase from the 20% to 30% of code AI currently produces at the company, and shows how rapidly Microsoft is moving to incorporate such technology. Then on Tuesday, Microsoft laid off more than a dozen engineers on Hulse’s team as part of a broader layoff of 6,000 people across the company that appeared to hit engineers harder than other types of roles, this person said. While the layoffs only affected 3% of staff and Microsoft publicly said the move was intended to reduce layers of management, six current and laid-off employees said executives have foreshadowed it for months as they talked up the imperative of boosting automation. Senior leaders across the company have been repeating a refrain to subordinates: Use AI to increase productivity in sales, engineering and customer support, among other roles. That’s in line with what Microsoft has been telling its enterprise customers—that Microsoft will be “customer zero” for the same AI it ispitching to them as a way to spend less moneyon employees. A Microsoft spokesperson said in a statement that the company is not replacing roles with AI but using technology to increase efficiency, and added that Microsoft will “continue to implement organizational changes necessary to best position the company for success.” The spokesperson added that, while Hulse and other leaders have encouraged staff to use AI more, there is no specific percent of code that staff are expected to generate using AI. The push shows the importance of Microsoft’s access to OpenAI’s industry-leading AI. Expanding that access is akey subject of current negotiations between the companies, which have numerous commercial ties. Software engineering is by far the biggest beneficiary of the most advanced AI, which appears to have reduced demand for junior engineers, at least for now, according to job listing site Indeed. In the case of Hulse’s team members, who patch bugs and fix outages in the company’s cloud-server unit, he told them to “become AI prompt engineers” who give instructions to an AI coding assistant, rather than traditional coders who write code from scratch, this person said.  Perhaps it’s no coincidence that software engineers made up around 40% of the people Microsoft laid off in its home state of Washington this week as part of the broader cuts, according to a state regulatory filing from the company. Doing More With Less Large enterprises have found that chatbots such as ChatGPT and Claudecan create code nearly as well as humansat much faster rates. AI developers such Anthropic, which makes Claude, have said the advent of AI coding could curtail their plans to hire coders in the future, while Amazon CEO Andy Jassy has said AI coding tools have saved thousands of hours and more than $260 million in labor costs. OpenAI on Friday released its most advanced coding assistant to automate complex software engineering tasks, and Google is planning a similar tool—both of which could help businesses do more work with fewer engineers. Other types of businesseshave also embraced AI as a way to save on head count costsas they come under pressure economically, though some automation efforts remain experimental. Tech companies have long been the earliest adopters of automation—especially firms that develop machine-learning algorithms. Google, for instance, for decades has steadily been automating core parts of its advertising business—including tools that proactively suggest and create ads for its customers—in ways that impacted staff. At Microsoft, some departments are developing AI that could theoretically take over employees’ roles in areas like customer support and sales, the current and former employees said. For instance, engineers in the Experiences and Devices group, which oversees Microsoft’s Office 365 software and AI Copilot products for businesses, have been developing an AI chatbot intended to handle customers’ technical support questions, according to two people involved in the effort. The tool, Help Agent, could reduce the need for customer support staff as well as those who write content for pages on Microsoft’s website to answer typical customer questions, the people said. Microsoft hasn’t yet finalized plans to release the Help Agent and hasn’t decided whether it would be a stand-alone product or a new feature within its existing Copilot chatbot, which is embedded in its Windows operating system and Edge browser, one of the people said. But ahead of that decision, the company on Tuesday laid off more than two dozen people working in corporate roles focused on customer support near its Redmond, Wash., campus, according to the state filing. Research managers have also told researchers to use AI code-writing software to come up with prototypes of new software products faster, the person said. title: Is Brian Chesky’s Big Bet Big Enough?

Welcome, Weekenders! In this newsletter:

• The Big Read: The AI euphoria—and peril—driving ServiceNow’s Bill McDermott

• The Top 5: Silicon Valley’s most exotic fitness goals

• Plus, our Recommendations: A wager to save a dad; “Fargo” in Maine; and a band of brothers from Down Under

Lately, I’ve lived exactly as Brian Chesky might want. Yet the experience has been deeply imperfect and a reflection of what could derail his megagrowth plans.

While visiting Mexico City last weekend, I filled a hole in a morning’s itinerary with a cooking class available on Airbnb’s Experiences feature. It was tremendous fun, with Vanessa, a chef in the megalopolis’ Roma neighborhood, dispensing age-old wisdom about tortillas (less masa is more), guacamole (add tomatillo) and dried-chile salsa (never spiced to the point of suffering, she insists).

I studied at Vanessa’s elbow just a couple days before Chesky unveiled a major revamp to Airbnb that hopes to turn it into a giant marketplace of bookings—a place to secure a massage, a photo shoot or a guided hike. The move greatly expands on Experiences, which since its 2016 launch has not lived up to Chesky’s expectations, and pushes Airbnb into micromarkets across the world. Thousands and thousands and thousands of Vanessas! And other small business owners like her who are eager to supplement their incomes. 

But I have some doubts about the plan (as does Ben Thompson), and the experience I’ve had with Airbnb since arriving in Los Angeles from Mexico City underscores a chief concern: I’m writing this from a West Hollywood apartment that sure looked nice from the pictures and cost nearly as much as a four-star hotel. Sitting here, though, I can only conclude those images benefited from some substantial amount of special effects magic. In reality, it is an aging, grimly appointed place; I picture some Raymond Chandler villain storming through the front door at any moment.

More than a decade into Airbnb’s existence, a booking on the app is still a total roll of the dice for the most part, and any frequent Airbnb user knows it. Sometimes it’s as advertised, but often it’s not. The inconsistency undoubtedly puts a limit on the customer base, a partial explanation as to why Airbnb hasn’t grown as much as Chesky has wanted recently.

If Airbnb hasn’t managed to solve the flaw in its core business, surely those new micromarkets will have the same problem—possibly in an exacerbated form since Airbnb wants to substantially broaden itself in unfamiliar settings and economies. How many people will pay for all these new services? I’m not saying the concept will be a total flop, but I can’t picture Airbnb making it work on a gigantic scale, which is what Chesky needs to goose the company’s stubbornly disappointing stock price.

And another thing—but, oh, my god, what is that stain on the wall, and why is it moving? 

What WBD’s Retreat Really Means 

A couple days ago, David Zaslav, the Warner Bros. Discovery chief, had to do what no one surely likes to do: publicly admit a mistake. But he did, and the company will re-rebrand (or is it a re-re-rebrand?) its streaming service, returning its name to HBO Max. 

The decision was mostly interpreted through a lens of what it reflects about WBD. That’s an amusingly narrow view, because if you pull back the camera, it also represents a pretty concrete final moment in the Streaming Wars. So yes, let’s just say it explicitly: Netflix has won. No other streamer—not Peacock, not HBO Max, not even Amazon—is going to come close to matching its enormous catalog. There’s Netflix, and then there’s everyone else, who I suspect would be best served by figuring out what makes them bespoke—or letting the end credits roll. 

Apple’s New Partner, Musk’s Old Rival 

The most interesting development at Apple isn’t a new iPhone or an update to its virtual reality headset: It’s the brain-computer interface Apple is reportedly developing with Synchron, a competitor to Elon Musk’s Neuralink. Our Akash Pasricha had a Big Read on Synchron a couple months ago, and the revelation about its partnership with Apple adds a substantial amount of legitimacy to Synchron’s efforts. At the same time, Apple’s decision to partner with Synchron rather than Neuralink puts another puncture in the perception of Musk as an unmatchable genius. Which, really, is happening more and more these days!—Abram Brown

Weekend’s Latest Stories

The Big Read 

Bots or Bust: ServiceNow’s Bill McDermott Makes an All-In Bet on AI

Bill McDermott, ServiceNow’s CEO, is someone who drafts off mile-high dreams, ones that at times seem to defy reality. Or as the company’s vice chair, Nick Tzitzon, put it: “Bill will never be constrained by what other people’s version of a situation is.”

His vision has come to rest solely on artificial intelligence, as our Akash Pasricha reports in Weekend’s latest Big Read. But McDermott faces something of an uphill climb. His salespeople have to convince customers they need ServiceNow’s AI—while every other company is trying to do the same with their AI—and then teach them how to use its unfamiliar features. McDermott sees the reinvention of the company as a total necessity. As he told Akash: “If you always do what you always did, you’ll always get what you always got.”

The Top Five

The Exotic Fitness Goals of the Tech Elite

When I was traveling over the past week, I felt proud of myself for sticking to my workout routine: a bunch of runs and even some early morning weightlifting at a gym near my dreary Airbnb. And then…I edited this humbling piece by our Nick Wingfield.

Nick tracked down a group of techies who’ve taken the same crazy drive that propels them at work and channeled it into some outlandish feats of fitness. They’re people who aren’t just satisfied they made it out for a couple miles: They measure their regimens in dozens of miles, which is exactly what Josh Ip, founder of Ranger, an AI startup, did to prepare for a self-organized 100-mile run around San Francisco last summer.

The run took Ip 29 hours to complete, and at different points, some of the investors in his startup ran alongside him. “Investors want you to be maniacal and tolerate any amount of pain. They also want to know you can run through walls,” Ip said. “If anything, me being able to do this was my way of showing, ‘Oh shit, this guy can do what he says he can do. If he can do that, I’m assuming he can build a startup.’” 

Abram Brown, editor of The Information’s Weekend section, has an unblemished Airbnb rating—in case you were wondering. Reach him at abe@theinformation.com.

Listening: “Embedded: Alternate Realities” (NPR) 

Generally, bets between family members are gentle affairs—wagers over bragging rights. Or a steak dinner at most. But the one NPR reporter Zach Mack made with his father in “Embedded: Alternate Realities” was different: Nominally, it carried a $10,000 prize. In reality, the stakes were even higher: They gambled over nothing less than the family’s ability to stay together. 

I’m not really reaching for hyperbole. Last year, Mack bet his father that 10 online conspiracy theories wouldn’t come true within a year—with Mack believing the strict timeline would be the only way to definitively prove them false to his father and prevent the family from breaking apart over his dad’s unshakable belief in them. Alas, the tale of a child trying to sober up a parent radicalized by the internet is an increasingly familiar one. Few are documented with such intimacy.—A.B.

Reading: “The Savage, Noble Death of Babs Dionne” by Ron Currie 

Imagine Maine, the state with “Vacationland” printed on license plates, and I promise whatever comes to mind is decidedly not the part of Maine ruthlessly controlled by Babs Dionne, a mother, grandmother and nightstick-wielding mobster. But Babs is losing her grip on her small-town turf, and over the course of the 24 hours presented in “The Savage, Noble Death of Babs Dionne,” it slips fully through her fingers. 

Mama Dionne has stretched her ambitions too far, enraging a rival outfit. In retaliation, her competitors dispatch a hitman known only as The Man, an Anton Chigurh of the north, who drives a spotless Impala rather than a pickup. To stave off The Man, Babs might hope to count on her military vet daughter, Lorie. But Lorie finds herself preoccupied by the ghostly apparitions of fallen comrades, possibly hallucinations from her spiraling opioid withdrawal. Like everyone around her, she is dogged by death and the deaths she’s caused.—A.B.

Watching: “The Narrow Road to the Deep North” (Amazon Prime)

Often, the hell of war is shown through gruesome scenes from the battlefield. That’s not really the case in “The Narrow Road to the Deep North,” which nonetheless makes war’s dire realities abundantly clear. The five-episode show is a domestic drama and a prisoner-of-war series, skipping between three timelines in the life of a young British doctor, Dorrigo Evans, who joins family in Australia before fighting against Japan in World War II, an experience that curdles him. Jacob Elordi, the tall hunk from “Euphoria” and “Saltburn,” plays Dorrigo in the two earlier periods; a weathered and excellent Ciarán Hinds follows behind him, portraying Dorrigo in the 1980s. Together, they present halves of the same broken person, fitting together remarkably well.—A.B.

Final Thought

You know—whatever works, folks!

title: The Exotic Fitness Goals of the Tech Elite

When normies want to set lofty fitness goals for themselves, they train for half- or full-marathons. If they’re feeling ambitious, perhaps they shoot for a triathlon or a Tough Mudder. For the type A personalities of tech, though, those events are sometimes warmups, literally, for even more extravagant athletic feats.

Last Friday night, for example, Randi Zuckerberg—an early Facebook employee and the host of a tech-themed radio show on SiriusXM—crossed the finish line in Flagstaff, Ariz., at the end of a 257-mile ultramarathon called the Cocodona 250. Zuckerberg said that 10 of the 16 marathons (26.2 miles) and 3 of the 10 ultramarathons (31 or more miles) she had run over the prior few years were part of her training regimen for the grueling Arizona race, which took her 113 hours to complete.

“The Boston Marathon I did as my final long run,” said Zuckerberg, who is the sister of Meta Platforms CEO Mark Zuckerberg.
content: When normies wantto set lofty fitness goals for themselves, they train for half- or full-marathons. If they’re feeling ambitious, perhaps they shoot for a triathlon or a Tough Mudder. For the type A personalities of tech, though, those events are sometimes warmups, literally, for even more extravagant athletic feats. Last Friday night, for example, Randi Zuckerberg—an early Facebook employee and the host of a tech-themed radio show on SiriusXM—crossed the finish line in Flagstaff, Ariz., at the end of a 257-mile ultramarathon called the Cocodona 250. Zuckerberg said that 10 of the 16 marathons (26.2 miles) and 3 of the 10 ultramarathons (31 or more miles) she had run over the prior few years were part of her training regimen for the grueling Arizona race, which took her 113 hours to complete. “The Boston Marathon I did as my final long run,” said Zuckerberg, who is the sister of Meta Platforms CEO Mark Zuckerberg. Doing hard athletic things has long been part of Silicon Valley’s ethos, providing an outlet to channel the competitiveness and boundary-pushing that’s in the bones of so many people in the industry. How, though, do you stand out from run-of-the-mill hypercompetitive tech fitness freaks? By finding even harder, more novel tests of physical resilience. I spoke to a handful of founders and investors to come up with a list of five of the gnarliest fitness challenges out there—and asked them how they achieved those feats. Running some of those gauntlets requires almost outlandish physical and mental endurance. Others are shorter tests of conditioning and strength. Sami Inkinen, co-founder of online real estate site Trulia, which Zillow bought for $2.5 billion in 2015, emphatically tackles endurance challenges. Between 2007 and 2018, he competed in more than two dozen full- and half-Ironman triathlons, ranking first in his age category multiple times. During summer 2014, Inkinen and his wiferowed, without additional support, 2,750 milesfrom California to Hawaii over 45 days. Earlier this year, Inkinen and a teammate completed the Absa Cape Epic, a brutal, eight-day mountain biking stage race in South Africa that covers around 400 miles and 54,000 feet of climbing. For Inkinen—now CEO and co-founder of Virta Health, a health tech startup—physically punishing exercise provides a mental escape from work. “If I only move my legs from one meeting to another, it’s such a limited experience,” he said Inkinen. “I love this feeling of using my body and limbs to be an animal out there. To me, that’s the full human experience.” Inside weight rooms, this club has become something like an unofficial badge of honor. To be a member, you simply have to lift a combination of weights totaling 1,000 pounds in three classic power-lifting moves: dead lift, squat and bench press. It’s up to the individual to decide how much weight to lift in each move. Chad Byers, founder and general partner at early-stage venture firm Susa Ventures, intends to join the 1,000-pound club, though he doesn’t plan to begin focusing exclusively on power lifting until July. As part of that effort, he’ll concentrate on gaining muscle mass and upping his intake of protein. Even if he succeeds in joining the club, he may fall short of his personal goal for the challenge. Traditionally, the 1,000-Pound Club requires only a single repetition for each move to qualify. But earlier this year, Byerscreated a listof his 2025 fitness goals in which he set his 1,000 Pound Club target at five reps, an audacious and perhaps unachievable number. “That’s exponentially harder,” said Byers. “That’s probably why I fucked up my list.” Hyrox has started to catch on globally among people who want to test their cardiovascular endurance and strength, with events in the U.S., Korea, Europe, India and the Middle East. It’s a timed event in which participants alternate between 1-kilometer runs and eight different workouts: SkiErg, sled push, sled pull, burpee broad jump, rowing, farmer’s carry, sandbag lunges and wall balls. It may sound like a lot, but Hyrox has become a popular alternative to CrossFit, which offers more varied high-intensity workouts generally requiring greater technical skill. Byers participated in his first Hyrox event in Miami in April and exceeded his goal of completing all of the challenges in under 1 hour and 30 minutes—by a hair, clocking in at 1 hour and 28 minutes. He trained for three months by doing heavy cardio workouts, including sprints, combined with a lot of strength training. He plans to do his second Hyrox event in Anaheim, Calif., in December, and hopes to finish it in less than 1 hour and 15 minutes. The most elite Hyrox athletes do the events in under an hour, but Byers knows his limits. “Sub one hour with my job is hard,” said Byers, whose firm has invested in Robinhood, Flexport and Human Interest. The Absa Cape Epic, which takes place on the southwestern coast of South Africa, is often described as the Tour de France of mountain biking, in part because teams of cyclists endure merciless climbing over a series of daylong stages. This year was the third time Inkinen has completed the race. His team of two came in seventh out of 149 teams in the master men’s category and 75th out of 532 teams overall. Conditions this year were rough, according to Inkinen. There were wild fluctuations in temperatures along the varied course, from 100 degrees Fahrenheit to frigid cold on rainy mountaintops where mud the consistency of peanut butter clogged his bike’s wheels. “I’m pretty sure I both cried and laughed at the same time on the way to the top,” he said. Training for the March race is a logistical challenge for Inkinen. He lives at over 8,000 feet in Colorado, which means snow conditions force him to mostly train on a stationary bike indoors in the months leading up to the race. Inkinen also travels a lot for work, so he sometimes ends up renting a bike to train outside, as he did in early March when he attended a tech conference in Arizona put on by investment bank Allen & Co. In total, he estimates he jams in 11 hours or more in the saddle per week: 1.5 hours a day in the early mornings of the workweek and 2 to 3 hours a day on the weekends. For Josh Ip—founder and CEO of Ranger, a startup thatuses artificial intelligence to quality-testsoftware code—the 100 mile distance was a magical number he couldn’t get out of his head. He belongs to San Francisco’s South End Rowing Club, an athletic club for swimmers, rowers, handball players and runners founded in 1873. One of Ip’s inspirations for his ultramarathon was a plaque on the wall of the club recognizing members who had run 100 miles, going back to 1979. But rather than enter an organized ultramarathon, Ip last summer simply did a 100-mile run on his own,looping aroundSan Francisco’s Presidio, Lands End and Fort Mason areas, traveling over the Golden Gate Bridge for another loop in the Marin Headlands, and then heading back to San Francisco. He said he’s not against organized races, but the solitude of doing his own ultramarathon was appealing. Still, he had help from friends, who helped pace him and supply him with high-caloric food, including salami and turkey sandwiches and mashed potatoes. Some of Ranger’s investors helped pace him too. “Investors want you to be maniacal and tolerate any amount of pain. They also want to know you can run through walls,” Ip said. “If anything, me being able to do this was my way of showing, ‘Oh shit, this guy can do what he says he can do. If he can do that, I’m assuming he can build a startup.’” The weirdest moment of the race happened at about 3 a.m.—around his 65th mile—when his headlamp caught the glowing eyes of a couple of animals on a trail in Marin: bobcats or possibly mountain lions. Ip completed the run, which he nicknamed the Dog 100, in 29 hours and 39 minutes, including breaks (the name is a reference to how friends tease Ip that he’s “got that dog” in him). To prepare, Ip put in a lot of miles, peaking at 70 miles a week. For him, the key to gutting out the 100-mile distance was going slow and keeping his heart rate as low as possible. “I’ve never cared about speed—only distance and how far you can push yourself,” said Ip, who kept himself focused by writing two words on his arm before his run: “patience” and “wisdom.” For the Cocodona 250, Zuckerberg also did not make speed a priority (up to a certain point: She needed to complete the race in under 125 hours to be considered a finisher). A lot of the terrain was so steep or rocky that it wasn’t runnable, said Zuckerberg, who spent stretches of it “power hiking.” She hurt her ankle around mile 190, which slowed her pace further. No one can complete a 257-mile race without racking up a lot of miles before the event, but Zuckerberg also found that sleep deprivation and nutrition were important elements in her training. The latter was crucial: She ended up sleeping a total of six hours over nearly five days during the race. For almost a year, Zuckerberg regularly set her alarm to go off every two hours in the middle of the night. She would then get up and run two miles, either on a treadmill or outdoors, as long as her husband or physical therapist could tag along. Then she’d head back to bed. Because ultrarunners burn a staggering number of calories during a race, many of them find it very difficult to eat enough without feeling like they’ve detonated a bomb in their stomachs. So Zuckerberg adopted a diet full of healthy fats ahead of the race to encourage her body to burn fat rather than carbs during the race. She says this helped her avoid stomach problems and “bonking,” a dreaded state of total fatigue that can derail endurance athletes. The day before the race, a body scan showed that Zuckerberg had a body fat reading of 19%. The day after, it was 13%. For moral support, Zuckerberg’s physical therapist and others helped pace her (when race rules allowed such help). Other friends formed the rest of her support crew, meeting her at aid stations along the route. Still, there were some dark moments. At around mile 230, she had to climb Mount Elden near Flagstaff. The altitude, lack of sleep and physical stress caught up to her. She had a moment of “full-body, hyperventilating crying” before collecting herself and finishing the race. “I felt I was in a videogame,” said Zuckerberg, who is the founder of Zuckerberg Media, a tech and media advising firm. “It was the final boss, and my life was blinking.” Nick Wingfield is features editor at The Information, where he has worked since 2018 after previously reporting on technology for The New York Times and Wall Street Journal. title: Why the Charter-Cox $34.5 Billion Cable Deal Matters

Misery loves company, as they say. Friday’s announcement that two of the three biggest cable-broadband firms, Charter Communications and Cox Communications, are combining is a logical next step in the consolidation of a stagnant but still significant industry. Malone, a star media dealmaker of the 1990s and early 2000s, is all but retired (the man once called the “Darth Vader” of cable last year gave up his nonvoting director emeritus position on Charter’s board). But the big cable companies are still the primary source of internet access for many, if not most, Americans, which makes them a little like the water company—a service people only think about when it doesn’t work. That makes their financial health important, given that they need to maintain the pipes that carry the internet to people’s homes and businesses. The backdrop is instructive. Cable’s original business of selling packages of TV channels has shrunk to a shadow of its former self. Selling internet access, which replaced TV as the industry’s growth engine, has peaked. In fact, Charter and Comcast have lately started losing internet customers, as phone companies like Verizon and T-Mobile have ramped up their internet-at-home services. The cable guys’ growth business now is selling mobile phone service, although they’re doing so by renting Verizon’s cellular network—even as they compete with Verizon and others for customers! The end result is that revenue growth in the past couple of years has been anemic for everyone in the industry, including the phone companies. Charter’s recent financial performance highlights the industry’s challenges. Its free cash flow shrank 30% between 2022 and 2024 as capital expenditures jumped while cash generated from its operations fell. To be sure, before this deal, Charter had forecast that its capex would start declining after this year, as big network upgrades come to an end. But the business is always going to be a capital-intensive one, which isn’t ideal given the lack of growth. Moreover, integrating Cox will eventually require some capital investment, Charter executives acknowledged Friday. The Cox acquisition creates some opportunities for growth. Cox, a smaller company by customers than Charter, hasn’t made anywhere near the inroads into mobile phone service that Charter has, for instance. Charter can change that. Its management hasn’t given up on rejuvenating sales of TV service, either, a business from which Cox has almost disappeared (it has only 1.7 million TV customers compared with 5.9 million broadband subscribers). Charter stock rose 1.8% in response to the deal. The only question is, how long can Charter eke out the gains from this combination? content: Qualcomm, known fordesigning and licensing smartphone processors, said earlier this week it would develop data center chips for artificial intelligence, starting in Saudi Arabia. The move adds Qualcomm to the long list of challengers to Nvidia, whose chips dominate the AI data center market. The little-noticed announcement came during a flood of press releases from the White House and American technology firms whose executives accompanied President Trump to the Middle East to warm up relations with leaders in the region. Qualcomm said it would work with Humain, a newly formed Saudi AI firm, to develop the new chips. Humain announced separate partnerships this week with rival chipmakers Nvidia and AMD to use their chips in its AI data centers. The Qualcomm announcement marks its official return to the data center market after prior efforts fizzled. Years ago, Qualcomm tried to take on Intel and Advanced Micro Devices by developing central processing units for data centers. Qualcomm then tried to break into the AI chip market in 2019but failedafter Facebook, a large potential customer, had concerns about the chip’s software.

title: Bots or Bust: ServiceNow’s Bill McDermott Makes an All-In Bet on AI
feed_content:
Late on a Friday night in March, Bill McDermott, ServiceNow’s CEO and chairman, walked off a flight in San Jose, Calif., and then immediately asked his chief of staff to get his top sales and engineering execs on the phone. He had a task for them.

McDermott had just spent a week in New York meeting with customers, including the heads of banks and a sports league. They’d told him they had no idea where to start with AI, which has become a matter of foremost importance to ServiceNow, a giant in the deeply unsexy business of making software for resolving issues in back-office departments such as IT, finance and HR. Many of the company’s latest programs involve AI, and McDermott has pinned a substantial portion of its growth to the technology—and to customers understanding its value.

In a 15-minute phone conversation with his lieutenants, McDermott outlined the details of a new AI consulting service for marquee clients that would arguably offer more hand-holding than any other such program offered by ServiceNow and gave them a tight deadline: He wanted it finalized in a couple weeks, so he could talk it up at ServiceNow’s 25,000-person customer conference at the Venetian Resort in Las Vegas.
content: Late on aFriday night in March, Bill McDermott, ServiceNow’s CEO and chairman, walked off a flight in San Jose, Calif., and then immediately asked his chief of staff to get his top sales and engineering execs on the phone. He had a task for them. McDermott had just spent a week in New York meeting with customers, including the heads of banks and a sports league. They’d told him they had no idea where to start with AI, which has become a matter of foremost importance toServiceNow, a giant in the deeply unsexy business of making software for resolving issues in back-office departments such as IT, finance and HR. Many of the company’s latest programs involve AI, and McDermott has pinned a substantial portion of its growth to the technology—and to customers understanding its value. In a 15-minute phone conversation with his lieutenants, McDermott outlined the details of a new AI consulting service for marquee clients that would arguably offer more hand-holding than any other such program offered by ServiceNow and gave them a tight deadline: He wanted it finalized in a couple weeks, so he could talk it up at ServiceNow’s 25,000-person customer conference at the Venetian Resort in Las Vegas. “On-site is insight: When you’re on-site, you have tremendous radar,” McDermott told me as we wended our way through a backstage area at the Venetian last week just after he had given his main address, which put a substantial spotlight on the consulting service. “Most companies play it cool. They’re always looking through a window, but they’re not necessarily on-site with their sleeves rolled up.” The service’s fast-paced development was quintessential McDermott, whose high-wire energy has gone up a few notches as AI fever has spread. As he well knows, everyone is selling AI these days. Or at least everyone istryingto sell it. (“There’s a lot of pretenders out there,” McDermott said.) But much of corporate America remains largely baffled by the technology, and it hasn’t been around long enough for companies to study it and determine whether it’s really worth it. So McDermott wants his people inside the companies adding his AI tools—to make sure they see their value and understand them. “The employee has to have a seamless experience: They don’t want to waste their time with 17 idiotic applications,” McDermott said. At the same time, software companies like ServiceNow have themselves faced questions about whether their customers might eventually be able to re-create much of what their products do using AI. I asked Amit Zavery, the company’s chief product and operating officer, whether such a scenario was a credible threat. He insisted it isn’t because ServiceNow’s software touches so many different departments within a customer’s business, which is perhaps true for now. McDermott, 63, has led ServiceNow since late 2019, a period of marked prosperity for the company. Annual revenue has more than tripled—reaching nearly $11 billion last year. Meanwhile, its share price has more than quadrupled, far outpacing the Nasdaq. Despite the fact that software companies are hardly household names, ServiceNow enjoys an almost cult-fan following among investors and customers. Attendees to the customer conference in Vegas swarmed McDermott, many of them asking him to take selfies with them. What has propelled ServiceNow in no small part is McDermott’s charm and skill as a consummate pitchman, who likes to have a thank-you note in an executive’s inbox within about an hour after a meeting. (“A salesperson to his bone,” as his chief financial officer, Gina Mastantuono, put it.) But the IT software he was selling a few years ago was much simpler than the AI offerings and was an easier product to sell.  Like many tech CEOs, he doesn’t have any choice: In the current moment, anyone who appears uneager to embrace AI risks being seen as sleepy and outdated. With the nascent AI era unfolding around him, McDermott finds himself at what might be the most pivotal point of his time at ServiceNow, and his ability to convince customers to buy AI could act as an industrywide weather vane: If he and his company can’t sell customers on AI and turn it into durable revenue, that would raise questions about how businesses with a less driven approach might fare. So far ServiceNow’s AI software, which can automatically resolve issues for IT, HR and finance teams, has quickly gained traction. As of May, its AI software had crossed $250 million in annual contract value, a measure of recurring revenue. By the end of 2026, the company expects the figure to hit $1 billion—a tall order. McDermott wouldn’t think about settling for anything less. “Bill believes that the situation—regardless of what it is—is so much bigger and more exciting” than what it might seem to someone else, said Nick Tzitzon, ServiceNow’s vice chair. Sometimes, though, McDermott’s hopes can sometimes seem to defy reality. “Bill will never be constrained by what other people’s version of a situation is.” If all goes according to plan, AI would still represent just a small portion of ServiceNow’s total revenue. Still, McDermott has rethought how his sales team operates, including changing their pay: ServiceNow partially compensates its sales team based on the extent to which customers use AI features, not just how many subscriptions they sell. Meanwhile, McDermott has chosen to devote himself almost entirely to evangelizing AI and his company’s efforts on the technology. In Vegas, he referred to it as nothing less than “the gateway to prosperity” and an “absolute requirement for survival.” McDermott’s boots-on-the-ground approachto winning customers with AI isn’t anything revolutionary for him. It’s the same mentality he used to sell photocopiers when he was at Xerox in the 1980s and 1990s. He later would spend nearly a decade at SAP, first as co-CEO and then as CEO, before joining ServiceNow in November 2019. He pushed ServiceNow to expand beyond its signature business—IT software—and release new tools for managing corporate finance, supply chains and compliance. To help customers understand what he wanted them to buy, he also grew the number of consulting firms ServiceNow worked with to show customers how to use its software, drawing on relationships he’d made in his SAP days. To clear the path for his salespeople, McDermott has tried to take more meetings with the CEOs of companies that might buy ServiceNow software than his predecessors typically did. He likes to be the initial evangelist and emissary with potential clients, and then he turns over the nitty-gritty discussions to his salespeople, who benefit from the foothold McDermott has given them. “It makes the conversation way easier,” said Adam Mansfield, an executive at UpperEdge, a consulting firm that helps businesses negotiate better deals on their contracts with ServiceNow. Mansfield told me McDermott has recently met with the CEOs at three of his customers running large companies, which wasn’t happening as often as it did a few years ago. (He wouldn’t comment on the identity of those companies, as he wishes to preserve his relationship with them.) McDermott’s sales team has the benefit of selling software many customers see as more cohesive and easier to use than what they might get elsewhere. Its various IT, HR and customer service tools are all hooked up to a single ServiceNow database, which can pull information customers have with other big data companies like Snowflake and Databricks. ServiceNow applications also work with all the major cloud providers, including Amazon Web Services and Microsoft Azure. AI hasn’t been ServiceNow’s sole preoccupation lately. Recently, the company has made its biggest push yet to compete with Salesforce, the sales and marketing software giant, by launching a variety of rival tools. Granted, the push has made some customers nervous that the company might be losing focus, Mansfield said. McDermott’s pitch to customers isn’t an especially novel one in software: It’s better and easier for them to get all their apps from one company rather than rely on a disparate array of programs from many different businesses. Asked about customers’ worries that the company might be stretching itself too thin, he responded with one of his usual bumper sticker–ready expressions. “If you always do what you always did,” he said, “you’ll always get what you always got.” When ChatGPT debutedin November 2022, McDermott joined his executives around a boardroom table and they played with the chatbot together. From there, he made a quick decision. “Bill’s like, ‘Let me make it clear to everybody here, everything you do: AI, AI, AI, AI, AI,’” recalled Tzitzon, the ServiceNow vice chair. To begin a customer meeting on AI, McDermott has asked his salespeople to do what amounts to their best impression of him: Present AI not as a matter of bots or databases but in grand-sounding terms, like “business transformation.” During the push to grow AI, McDermott has insisted his managers improve efficiency across their teams. He is laser-focused on a sales team’s participation rate. “Let’s assume you’re a manager, and you have 12 direct reports,” he said. “Now let’s assume out of those 12, two people did good, which wassogood that the manager was 110% of plan. I don’t think that’s good. I tell the manager: ‘What did the other 10 do?’” The product they’re selling goes for a big markup over older software. Before ServiceNow started adding AI features, it offered customers two subscription plans, Standard and Pro. Now it has a third, Pro Plus, which contains the AI features and costs about 30% more than Pro. Pro Plus comes with a strict limit on how much customers can use AI, but they can pay more for additional access. Michael Park, a ServiceNow senior vice president who helps lead AI sales and consulting, framed the new pricing model to me as a blessing, not a burden: It gives his salespeople an excuse to check in with existing customers and see if they can sell them more AI before their yearslong contracts end. I asked Mansfield, the executive at the firm that helps businesses negotiate with ServiceNow, what feedback he’d gotten on how effective ServiceNow’s AI was at actually improving a company’s operations. “I would say we are in the feeling-it-out, too-early-to-tell period,” he said. To be sure, few companies have publicly put dollar values on the benefit they’re seeing from ServiceNow’s AI. Canadian phone carrier Bell is one exception: It says it is saving $1 million every year on support calls with customers using ServiceNow’s chatbots. (ServiceNow, for its part, said it will save roughly $100 million itself using its own AI in 2025.) At the same time, other customers acknowledge they’re seeing significant time savings. Perkins Coie, a law firm with over 1,200 attorneys, has used ServiceNow’s AI software to resolve nearly 20,000 hourslong tickets in two-thirds the time, according to Jeremy Newman, Perkins Coie’s director of IT customer service. And AstraZeneca, the pharma giant, has said it will save 90,000 hours onboarding employees across the company. One thing is for sure, though: McDermott’s salespeople sure seem to have picked up on his urgency—and bought firmly into his schtick. Shortly after I returned from seeing McDermott in Vegas and attending ServiceNow’s conference, a ServiceNow salesperson rang me out of the blue, apparently assuming I was a potential customer. He asked me whether I had liked the event, and I later asked him what he thought about his CEO. “Oh, my god,” he said, before launching into a lengthy litany of praise for McDermott. He even liked McDermott’s choice of corporate tagline, which is likely indecipherable to anyone unfamiliar with the business but appears on much of its marketing material: “DESCO21C,” which translates to “defining enterprise software company of the 21st century.” I asked him if he thought the slogan was clunky at all. His response would surely please McDermott: “It keeps you going knowing you’re on a rocket ship.” Akash Pasricha leads data reporting for The Information Pro and manages the publication's Org Charts franchise. He covers AI and venture capital, enterprise software and IPOs, and all-things creator economy. Reach him at[email protected]or on X: @akashpasricha.

content: Two of thebiggest cable TV and broadband operators, Charter Communications and Cox Communications, are combining, in a sign of how the decline of cable TV and competition in broadband is forcing another stage of consolidation. Charter is buying Cox in a deal that values Cox at $34.5 billion, including $12.6 billion of net debt. Cox Enterprises, the family-owned media conglomerate that controls Cox Communications, will receive $21.9 billion in cash and stock. The combined company will have 35.9 million internet customers and about 14 million TV customers, making it a bit bigger than Comcast Corp., now the biggest firm in the industry. Cable TV was once the core business of cable operators but that business has shrunk in recent years, as consumers have defected to cheaper streaming services. That has made internet-access the core business, although growth in signing up new internet customers has stopped and cable operators are now losing customers to mobile phone companies.
